result:
Somewhere between the first cup of coffee and the late afternoon, curiosity usually knocks. It may arrive disguised as a question, a half-finished sketch, or the urge to walk down a street I have never taken. These impulses are small lanterns. Follow one long enough, and it can illuminate an entire unfamiliar world.

I like the feeling of not knowing exactly what comes next. Books do this beautifully: a sentence opens a door, and behind it waits an argument, a landscape, or a person whose decisions suddenly seem less foolish and more human. Travel does it too, though with fewer instructions. A wrong turn can become the most memorable part of the journey.

Certain people possess curiosity like a natural resource. They ask obvious questions that experts have forgotten to ask. They examine ordinary objects as if archaeological discoveries might hide inside. Around them, dull routines become playful, and strangers become potential friends.

Perhaps curiosity is simply attention with an adventurous accent. It asks us to linger, question, and connect. It also protects us from taking certainty too seriously. The person who assumes they know everything has closed the door before the interesting room appears.

So today I will leave one question unresolved. I will follow a side path, read beyond the familiar page, and speak to someone new. Not because certainty has become dangerous, but because wonder still feels like a gift. And gifts are easier to appreciate when the hands remain open. That is enough reason to begin.
